summary: Discovery to align on unit economics constraints for a conversational assistant product. Customer constrained by a hard monthly budget; evaluating hosted for speed of rollout, dedicated for predictable throughput, private for data residency. Primary levers discussed: batching, prefix/KV caching, model quantization, and routing fallbacks. Agreed to exchange traffic profile and run benchmark pilot.
topics: KV/prefix caching impact on unit cost
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Nora (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:05] Ellen: Ellen here.
[00:00:06] Jonah: Jonah on the line.
[00:00:08] Priya: Priya here.
[00:00:10] Nora: Great. Marcus from our infra team is with me, he'll cover the deeper perf bits. Marcus?
[00:00:15] Marcus (SE): Hi all, thanks. I'll try to stay pragmatic — ready to go into batching, kv cash and quant notes, sorry kv cache, my bad.
[00:00:25] Ellen: No worries. To kick off, our PM sent a one-pager: we have a hard cap of $35k / month for inference, runway is three months to validate. We need something that is close to production day-one and that won't blow budget.
[00:00:40] Nora: Understood. When you say $35k, is that for dev+prod combined or just prod inference?
[00:00:47] Ellen: Mostly prod inference. We'll keep a small dev sandbox but it's negligible.
[00:00:52] Jonah: For context, our assistant gets medium-length prompts, about 120 tokens input, 180 tokens output on average right now. Peak QPS is around 45, baseline 8. We'll share a histogram.
[00:01:05] Marcus: That's super helpful. Off the cuff, model choice and batching strategy will move the needle 2-5x on unit cost. Also caching prefixes for repeated prompts can cut token generation substantially.
[00:01:18] Priya: The other constraint is data residency — certain PII routes must stay in our VPC, so private deployments are on the table. But we don't want 0 ops teams to manage infra for months.
[00:01:30] Nora: Right, so tradeoffs: hosted = fastest, lowest ops; dedicated = reserved capacity for predictable throughput/cost; private = we install in your VPC/on-prem for residency but with more ops. We'll walk through levers that affect per-token pricing.
[00:01:45] Marcus: Let me sketch the levers — one, model size and quantization (q4 vs q8bis etc) changes GPU utilization; two, continuous batching vs strict single-request latency windows; three, KV/prefix caching which avoids re-generating common completions; four, routing to cheaper model variants on non-critical requests.
[00:02:03] Jonah: Quick question — when you say routing cheaper variants, do you mean automatically fall back to a smaller model? How would that affect latency and coherence of output?
[00:02:12] Marcus: Yes, we can route by policy. For low criticality queries we might use a smaller 7B quantized model, for high SLAs we use a 13B or 70B float. We aim to maintain coherence by white listing prompt types for fallback. Latency usually improves with smaller models, cost drops significantly but quality can vary.
[00:02:30] Ellen: Can you give me a sense in dollars? Like if we do hosted with a mid-tier model and modest batching, how does that translate to a per-1k-token cost?
[00:02:40] Nora: We typically present scenarios. Rough benchmarks: hosted w/ optimized kernel mid-model could be in the range of $0.30 - $0.90 per 1k tokens depending on batch and cache hit rate. With dedicated and reserved capacity you often get lower unit cost at scale — maybe down to $0.12 - $0.40 per 1k tokens — because fixed GPU op cost is amortized. Private can be comparable to dedicated after infra cost accounting, but upfront setup and ops raise the initial effective rate.
[00:03:05] Priya: Those are ranges. What's KV cache hit realistic expectation? Our templates reuse a lot of system prompts and helper sequences.
[00:03:12] Marcus: If set up well, prefix/KV caching can lead to 20-60% token savings for template-heavy workloads. It depends on prompt diversity. With a high reuse of system snippets, we often see ~40% reduction on generation tokens. But cache warms gradually.
[00:03:28] Jonah: And batching: we have a 50ms tail latency requirement for some real-time flows. How much batching will hurt that?
[00:03:35] Marcus: There's always a latency/cost trade. Continuous batching groups requests opportunistically — if you can accept a small queuing window (e.g., 10-20ms), you can achieve 2-3x better throughput per GPU. If you need strict 50ms p95, batching window must be tiny, which reduces batching efficiency and raises cost.
[00:03:53] Ellen: So if we keep 50ms p95 for real-time, we should expect higher per-token cost for those endpoints and route less critical tasks to cheaper models with heavier batching.
[00:04:03] Nora: Exactly. That's a common pattern: multi-tier routing. We'll show a pilot config that splits traffic by route.
[00:04:08] Priya: About encryption and keys: we use AWS KMS and would need to ensure keys never leave our account. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[00:04:16] Nora: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we support KMS/HSM integration. Hosted API can use envelope encryption with customer-supplied keys for some artifacts; we'll follow up with our KMS integration doc.
[00:04:26] Jonah: Any limitations on quantized models for accuracy-sensitive flows? We saw some hallucination sensitivity with aggressive quantization in earlier tests.
[00:04:34] Marcus: True — very aggressive quantization (e.g., int4 mixed) can impact factuality in edge cases. That's why part of the pilot is A/Bing quality on the same prompts: compare q4_0 against q8fine and a float baseline. We can baseline with your golden prompts.
[00:04:48] Ellen: Can you summarize a concrete pilot? What will you run, and how will we measure cost impact?
[00:04:54] Marcus: Pilot scope suggestion: 7-day run with your anonymized traffic replay at a 10% sampling. We'll spin a dedicated pool for that run and run three configs: hosted-like (no KV cache, minimal batching), optimized-batched + KV cache enabled, and fallback-routing mix (smaller model for non-critical routes). We'll measure tokens generated, cache hits, latency SLOs, and compute cost.
[00:05:15] Nora: We'll also provide a cost projection model so you can plug in expected QPS and cache hit rates to estimate monthly spend.
[00:05:22] Priya: Ops question — if we go dedicated, how are upgrades handled? Kernel/runtime patches?
[00:05:27] Marcus: For Dedicated we manage the runtime and orchestrate upgrades with canary deploys. You get control plane visibility; we coordinate maintenance windows. For Private, there's an option: Redwood-managed private (we operate inside your VPC) or customer-operated (we ship a package and your team applies updates).
[00:05:42] Ellen: About legal and audit logs: we need full request logs for debugging but PII redaction enforced. How do you handle retention?
[00:05:49] Nora: We support configurable retention policies and can redact PII at ingestion or provide token-level masking. We'll send the security whitepaper; SOC2 status is in there.
[00:05:58] Jonah: Slight transcription note: previously vendor docs called KV cash in a slide, haha.
[00:06:02] Nora: (laughs) okay noted.
[00:06:05] Ellen: One more on pricing: if we assume 2M tokens/day, 30% cache hit, and mixed routing with 20% on smaller model, can you sketch monthly cost?
[00:06:16] Marcus: Rough calc: 2M tokens/day -> 60M tokens/month. If 30% saved by cache -> 42M billable tokens. If 20% are routed to a cheaper model with unit cost 0.15/1k and the rest at 0.45/1k, blended ~ ((0.2*42M*0.00015) + (0.8*42M*0.00045)) * 1k? Let me reframe: per 1k tokens formula. Quickly: cheaper path cost ~ $0.15/1k -> 0.15 * (0.2*42k) = hmm rehearsed math is messy on the call, we'll send exact spreadsheet.
[00:06:49] Jonah: Yeah send the calc, we'll plug our numbers.
[00:06:52] Nora: We'll send both spreadsheet scenarios and a concise one-page cost summary.
[00:06:56] Priya: How long does dedicated provisioning take? If we sign a committed reserve, what's lead time?
[00:07:02] Nora: For typical pools it's 2-4 weeks to provision and tune; committed contracts expedite capacity reservation and SLA. Private deployments can take longer due to network and security approvals — often 4-8 weeks depending on approvals.
[00:07:14] Ellen: That's helpful. Our timeline: decision by end of quarter, pilot must start within three weeks.
[00:07:20] Nora: We'll prioritize the pilot and aim to have proposed configs and pricing by Friday 2026-10-22.
[00:07:25] Jonah: Cool. Small nit: can we see token-level latency percentiles? p50/p95/p99?
[00:07:30] Marcus: Yes; Redwood Console exposes per-route p50/p95/p99 and token breakdown. We'll include sample screenshots.
[00:07:36] Ellen: Any tricky gotchas we should watch for?
[00:07:38] Marcus: Cold-start KV misses, prompt drift that reduces cache effectiveness, and tail latency spikes when model compaction triggers background IO. We'll propose mitigations in the pilot config.
[00:07:49] Priya: For KMS, we need a diagram of key flow.
[00:07:52] Nora: Will include that in the security packet. Link: https://redwood.ai/security-integration (note: demo link, full doc to follow).
[00:07:58] Jonah: And samples of the billing output? We want line items that show tokens, model SKU, GPU-hours.
[00:08:03] Nora: We'll include sample billing export and nightly cost breakdown.
[00:08:07] Ellen: Great. Recap?
[00:08:09] Nora: Recap: 1) Velvet sends anonymized 7-day traffic & top prompts (Ellen). 2) Redwood sends pricing scenarios and security/KMS docs (Nora). 3) Marcus sets up pilot config and spreadsheet for cost calc (Marcus). 4) Schedule deep bench week of 10/25.
[00:08:26] Ellen: That aligns. Thanks all.
[00:08:29] Nora: Thanks, we'll follow up via email and calendar invite.
[00:08:33] [call ends]
